lessons.title: Map scale, direction and grid references
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Map work and practical skills (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use a scale to convert map distance to ground distance and the reverse
Give directions with compass points and bearings
Give and read four- and six-figure grid references
reviewNotes: Teacher to check which map style and conventions (four- vs six-figure references, bearings) the GCE Board's map-work paper uses.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **scale** tells us how much smaller the map is than the ground. A **representative fraction** such as 1 : 50 000 means that 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm (500 m, or 0.5 km) on the ground. A **statement scale** says it in words (1 cm to 1 km) and a **linear scale** is a ruler line drawn on the map.

blocks.caption: The eight compass points
blocks.alt: A compass rose with eight arrows labelled N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W and NW.

blocks.title: Measuring distance
blocks.md:
1. Measure the map distance in cm with a ruler (use a string for curved roads or rivers).
2. Multiply by the scale number (50 000 for 1 : 50 000).
3. Convert cm to km: divide by 100 000.
Example: 6.4 cm on a 1 : 50 000 map is 6.4 × 50 000 = 320 000 cm = 3.2 km.

**Direction:** the eight main compass points are N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW. For more accuracy we use a **bearing**, an angle from north measured clockwise: north is 000°, east 090°, south 180° and west 270°. On most maps north is at the top.

blocks.title: Grid references
blocks.md: Vertical lines (eastings) are numbered across the bottom of the map; horizontal lines (northings) up the side. In a **four-figure reference** give the eastings number first, then the northings number of the square's lower-left corner. In a **six-figure reference** divide the square into tenths to give a more exact position. Remember: along the corridor, then up the stairs.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Giving the northings before the eastings.
- Forgetting to convert cm to km.
- Measuring a bearing anticlockwise; it is always clockwise from north.
- Confusing a larger scale (1 : 25 000, more detail) with a smaller scale (1 : 500 000, less detail).

blocks.title: Example 1: map distance to ground distance
blocks.statement: On a map of scale 1 : 50 000 two villages are 6.4 cm apart. Find the ground distance in km.

blocks.title: Example 2: grid reference
blocks.statement: A school lies in the square whose lower-left corner is at easting 24 and northing 71. Give the four-figure reference.
steps: Join them without a space or comma.

objectives: Recognise steep and gentle slopes, valleys, spurs and peaks from contours
Draw and interpret a cross-section and check intervisibility

blocks.md: A **contour line** joins places that have the same height above sea level. The **contour interval** is the vertical height between two lines (for example 20 m). Heights on a map are measured from sea level. A **spot height** gives the exact height of a point and a **trig point** is a surveyed marker on a summit.

items.text: Steep slope: contours close together on the left

blocks.caption: Contour lines on a hill (schematic)
blocks.alt: Concentric rings that are close together on the left side and wide apart on the right.

blocks.title: Reading the shape of the land
blocks.md:
- Contours **close together**: steep slope. **Far apart**: gentle slope.
- Closed rings with higher numbers inside: hill or peak.
- **V-shapes pointing uphill** mark a valley (a river runs in it).
- Contours bulging downhill mark a **spur**.
- Evenly spaced lines: uniform slope.
- A sudden merging of lines: cliff or escarpment.

blocks.title: Gradient
blocks.md: Gradient = vertical interval ÷ horizontal distance, with both in the same unit. A rise of 100 m over 3 000 m gives 100 ÷ 3 000, or 1 in 30.

A **cross-section** is a side view along a line drawn between two points. To draw it: lay a strip of paper along the line, mark each contour crossing with its height, transfer the marks to graph paper, plot the heights, and join the points smoothly. Use a suitable vertical scale and label the axes. Two places are **intervisible** if no higher ground lies in between on the section.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Contour lines never cross (except at a cliff).
- Do not join the ends of the profile with straight lines; the real land is curved.
- Vertical exaggeration makes slopes look steeper on the section than they are; state the vertical scale.

blocks.title: Example 1: calculate gradient
blocks.statement: Point A is at 100 m and point B is at 400 m. The horizontal distance between them is 3 km. Find the gradient as 1 in n.

blocks.title: Example 2: steep or gentle?
blocks.statement: Along the line PQ the 100 m and 200 m contours are 1 cm apart; along the line RS they are 4 cm apart on the same map. Which line is steeper?
steps: The same height change happens over a shorter distance on PQ.
A shorter horizontal distance for the same rise means a steeper slope.
So PQ is steeper than RS.
